missing_spec_content.spec_text: One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre. 1 joule = 1 newton-metre
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives W = Fd with the unit joules. It never defines the joule in terms of 1 N moving through 1 m, and never states 1 J = 1 N m.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to convert between newton-metres and joules.
missing_spec_content.why: Newton-metres are not mentioned anywhere in the lesson, so this conversion is not taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never links work done against friction to a temperature rise.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe the energy transfer involved when work is done.
missing_spec_content.why: keyPoints[3].content only says 'When a force acts through a distance, energy is transferred.' It does not describe which energy stores change, for example kinetic to thermal by friction, or into gravitational potential energy when lifting.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Power is defined as the rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done.
missing_spec_content.why: The definition in keyPoints[0].content and keyTerms gives only 'the rate of energy transfer'. The second half of the definition, 'the rate at which work is done', is never stated in words. Only the equation P = W/t appears.

above_gcse.text: Power can also be written as: P = Fv (power = force × velocity). This comes from P = W/t = Fd/t = F × (d/t) = Fv.
above_gcse.why: P = Fv is not in the specification sections supplied. It is an A-level equation. A whole key point, a checkpoint, a common mistake, an exam tip and a revision card are built on it, which could lead the student to think it must be recalled.

above_gcse.text: A car engine produces a driving force of 4000 N at a speed of 25 m/s. What is the engine's power output?
above_gcse.why: This checkpoint tests P = Fv, which is beyond the specification sections supplied.

above_gcse.text: For P = Fv questions, check the units: newtons × metres per second = watts.
above_gcse.why: This implies that P = Fv questions are set at this level. The supplied specification does not include this equation.

above_gcse.text: Adding force and velocity instead of multiplying in P = Fv.
above_gcse.why: This common mistake depends on the above-specification equation P = Fv.

above_gcse.text: P = Fv (power = force × velocity). Useful for vehicles at constant speed
above_gcse.why: This puts an above-specification equation on the revision card as if it must be learned.

factual_errors.text: Triangle trick: put P at the top, and E and t at the bottom.
factual_errors.correction: Because P = E/t (so E = P × t), E goes at the top of the triangle and P and t go at the bottom. With P at the top, covering P would give E × t, which is wrong.

factual_errors.text: A professional Tour de France cyclist can keep up about 400 W for an hour. That is impressive, but far less than even a small electric motor.
factual_errors.correction: Many small electric motors (toys, fans, small appliances) are rated well below 400 W. 400 W is not 'far less than even a small electric motor'.

factual_errors.text: But the crane that does it in 5 seconds has four times the power. P = E/t, so for the same E, halving t doubles P.
factual_errors.correction: The 'four times' figure is correct, because the time is divided by 4 (20 s to 5 s). The explanation given, 'halving t doubles P', does not explain a factor of four. Dividing t by 4 multiplies P by 4.

wrong_terms.spec_term: W = F s (distance, s, 'distance moved along the line of action of the force')

wrong_terms.text: Work done W = Fd. Force (N) × distance (m) = joules (J)
W = Fd; energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance
Work done W = Fd (force × distance); unit: joules (J)

wrong_terms.spec_term: the rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done

not_checked: Checkpoints are keyed '1' and '3' and there is no checkpoint '2'. It is unclear whether these keys are 0-indexed or 1-indexed. If 1-indexed, checkpoint '3' (P = Fv) would sit with keyPoints[2] 'Power in everyday contexts', which does not support its answer. If 0-indexed, it matches keyPoints[3]. Under both readings, checkpoint '1' (P = E/t) is supported by the equation in keyPoints[0] or keyPoints[1].

The approximate everyday power values (body at rest ~80 W, walking ~300 W, running ~500–800 W, cycling 100–400 W) appear to mix metabolic power with mechanical output. These are estimates and were not checked precisely.
All keyPoints have diagram: null, so there were no diagrams or images to check.
